review.correction: State fixed replica-set, completed-write and version-order assumptions. Overlap alone is not a general linearizability proof; concurrent/incomplete writes and clock skew need protocols.

review.issue: Program-order preservation called linearizability; three session properties equated with it.
review.correction: Linearizability additionally respects real-time precedence across clients. Session guarantees are weaker; present them separately.

review.issue: HDFS, BigTable and S3 all described as DHT filesystems.
review.correction: Treat these as different distributed storage designs. Avoid asserting common hash routing or filesystem semantics without product-specific evidence.

exercise.prompt: A key has three replicas. Compare R=2,W=2 with R=1,W=3 when one replica becomes unreachable. State what you can and cannot conclude about consistency.
exercise.answer: Both choices satisfy R+W>N, so successful read and write quorums overlap in the simple fixed-replica model. With one unreachable replica, R=2,W=2 can still meet both quorums; R=1,W=3 can read but cannot complete its configured write quorum. Overlap alone is not a proof of linearizability. Discuss version ordering, concurrent writes, repair, and the failure assumptions.

units.title: Choosing a data store
units.description: Choose storage by workload and correctness requirements, from transactions to analytics, search, documents, and objects.

chapters.title: Start with workload and invariants
paragraphs: Choose storage by describing the application’s operations before choosing a product. Record the shape and size of the data, lookup keys, range queries, joins, update rates and required guarantees. Course registration needs to protect seat counts; lecture recordings need efficient delivery of large objects; course notes may need ranked text search. One application can have several distinct storage workloads.

A product category is a starting point, not a complete decision. Relational schemas can evolve, document stores can validate fields, and many systems combine capabilities. Evaluate the operations that must be atomic, the acceptable staleness and the team’s operational constraints. Using several stores is useful only when their ownership and update paths are clear enough to maintain.
chapters.prediction: Should video files and seat reservations necessarily use the same persistence interface?
chapters.explanation: No. Large-object delivery and concurrent invariant-preserving updates have different access patterns and can justify different stores.
chapters.narration: Choose storage by describing the application’s operations before choosing a product Record the shape and size of the data, lookup keys, range queries, joins, update rates and required guarantees. No. Large-object delivery and concurrent invariant-preserving updates have different access patterns and can justify different stores.

chapters.title: Transactions and concurrency
paragraphs: A checkout updates several related facts: the order, its line items and the remaining gift-card balance. Atomicity means these changes commit together or roll back together. It does not, by itself, make a read-then-write sequence safe from another checkout. Two transactions can read the same balance and compute competing replacements unless the chosen isolation or update protocol prevents it.

One approach locks the gift-card row before checking and changing the balance. Another performs a conditional decrement that succeeds only when sufficient balance remains, checks the affected-row result and keeps the order changes in the same transaction. The application must handle conflicts and rollback. A hand-written distributed spin lock is not a substitute: it also needs ownership, expiry and crash-recovery semantics.
chapters.prediction: Does adding BEGIN and COMMIT to the slide’s plain SELECT then overwrite necessarily stop double spending?
chapters.explanation: No. The operation needs appropriate isolation, locking or an atomic conditional update, plus balance validation and failure handling.
chapters.narration: A checkout updates several related facts: the order, its line items and the remaining gift-card balance Atomicity means these changes commit together or roll back together. No. The operation needs appropriate isolation, locking or an atomic conditional update, plus balance validation and failure handling.

chapters.title: Storage models and analytics
paragraphs: Operational transaction processing usually consists of many small reads and writes, such as fetching a student’s enrolments or reserving a seat. Analytics may scan years of records to compare enrolment trends. A column-oriented layout can read just the relevant columns and compress similar values effectively, making it attractive for broad aggregations over large datasets.

This distinction concerns workloads, not an absolute ban on indexes or a requirement that every analytical query use many machines. Analytical copies may be refreshed through ingestion pipelines and lag behind operational state. Explain that freshness before using a dashboard for an immediate decision. Running aggregation near storage also avoids sending every raw row to the application merely to calculate a small result.
chapters.prediction: For a three-year average grouped by location, why might reading columns beat fetching complete rows?
chapters.explanation: The calculation needs only selected attributes, so reading and compressing those columns can reduce I/O substantially.
chapters.narration: Operational transaction processing usually consists of many small reads and writes, such as fetching a student’s enrolments or reserving a seat Analytics may scan years of records to compare enrolment trends. The calculation needs only selected attributes, so reading and compressing those columns can reduce I/O substantially.

chapters.title: Documents, search and wide-column stores
paragraphs: A document store can keep a nested profile as one aggregate, with a configured shard key controlling distribution. A search engine serves another need: locating documents by terms and relevance. An inverted index maps each term to matching document identifiers. A query for Watertown AND gift intersects those posting lists instead of scanning every document’s text.

Wide-column and key-value designs are often shaped around known partition keys and within-partition ordering. Sensor readings might group by device and a bounded time interval, then order by timestamp. A good design considers partition size and hot devices as well as lookup convenience. Product feature lists in the source are historical; the durable lesson is to align the storage abstraction with the actual query.
chapters.prediction: How would a basic inverted index answer a two-term AND query?
chapters.explanation: Find the document-ID list for each normalized term and return their intersection.
chapters.narration: A document store can keep a nested profile as one aggregate, with a configured shard key controlling distribution A search engine serves another need: locating documents by terms and relevance. Find the document-ID list for each normalized term and return their intersection.

chapters.title: Caches and memory data structures
paragraphs: An application cache stores values that help construct responses, such as a leaderboard or precomputed summary. An HTTP reverse-proxy cache stores reusable responses at a different layer. These may coexist: an uncached personalized page can still reuse a cached shared fragment. Define which store owns the authoritative data and how cached copies expire or are invalidated.

In-memory systems can expose structures such as sets, counters and sorted sets, reducing the work required to update a small part of a value. Persistence, expiry and eviction depend on configuration; they are not determined solely by calling a product a cache. A rebuildable cache and a durable database have different recovery requirements even when they use the same software.
chapters.prediction: If a leaderboard cache disappears, should authoritative course records disappear too?
chapters.explanation: No. If it is designed as a rebuildable cache, the source records remain elsewhere and the leaderboard can be recomputed.
chapters.narration: An application cache stores values that help construct responses, such as a leaderboard or precomputed summary An HTTP reverse-proxy cache stores reusable responses at a different layer. No. If it is designed as a rebuildable cache, the source records remain elsewhere and the leaderboard can be recomputed.

chapters.title: Files, objects and final selection
paragraphs: A mounted network filesystem provides a file interface that existing applications can use. Block storage instead exposes volumes on which a filesystem may be built; object storage exposes named objects through service APIs. These are distinct abstractions. EFS is file storage, while EBS is block storage. Object storage is a natural fit for lecture media addressed through delivery URLs.

Distributed processing historically benefits from moving computation close to data, as illustrated by HDFS. Other designs separate compute and object storage, so locality is one consideration rather than a universal requirement. Finish the selection with a small architecture: identify the owner of each dataset, the access path, consistency needs and recovery process, then explain why a simpler arrangement would or would not suffice.
chapters.prediction: Can an application replace any mounted filesystem with an object bucket without changing behavior?
chapters.explanation: Not necessarily. It must check required file operations and semantics against the object API and adapt its access pattern.
chapters.narration: A mounted network filesystem provides a file interface that existing applications can use Block storage instead exposes volumes on which a filesystem may be built; object storage exposes named objects through service APIs. Not necessarily. It must check required file operations and semantics against the object API and adapt its access pattern.

quiz.question: Why does START TRANSACTION plus reading a balance into a variable not by itself prevent two checkouts from overspending?
quiz.answer: Atomicity does not guarantee the required isolation. Both may read the same value; use locking or an atomic conditional decrement with balance checks and rollback behavior.

quiz.question: How can a search index answer Watertown AND gift?
quiz.answer: Store a posting list of document IDs for each term, then intersect the two lists; index analysis and normalization determine token matching.

quiz.question: Choose stores for lecture videos, seat reservations and full-text notes search. Explain one reason for each.
quiz.answer: Object storage for large media objects; a transactional database for seat-count invariants; a search engine/inverted index for text retrieval. Integrate them with explicit ownership and update propagation.

review.issue: Repeats CAP/session guarantees errors.
review.correction: Apply the DB 2 corrections: CAP is conditional on partition, and session guarantees are not linearizability.

review.issue: EBS listed as a network filesystem.
review.correction: EBS is block storage; EFS is file storage. Keep object, file and block abstractions distinct.

review.issue: SQL requires all writes on one master.
review.correction: Describe the single-primary relational design in the slides rather than every SQL system. SQL is a query language and relational data model does not dictate one write topology.

review.issue: Gift-card transaction claims atomicity prevents double spend, but plain SELECT then overwrite races.
review.correction: Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with balance validation, or an atomic conditional UPDATE balance=balance-amount WHERE balance>=amount and check affected rows within the order transaction; handle rollback/retry.

review.issue: Distributed transactions must lock all replicas; naive CAS spin lock offered without failure behavior.
review.correction: Present distributed transaction protocols as product-dependent. The sketch lacks leases, fencing, backoff and crash recovery and must not be offered as production code.

review.issue: _id always sharding key; journaling preserves document history.
review.correction: The shard key is configured and need not be _id. Journaling supports crash recovery, not application version history.

review.issue: Ancient product/version and licensing tables presented as current.
review.correction: Label those tables historical and replace with durable design trade-offs. Do not repeat current licensing/protocol/feature claims without checking current vendor docs.

review.issue: NoSQL always disk/persistent, caches always expiring, network filesystems obsolete.
review.correction: These are workload defaults rather than definitions. TTL/persistence/eviction are configurable product policies; file APIs remain appropriate when filesystem semantics are needed.

exercise.prompt: Choose storage roles for an online course service with enrolments, uploaded videos, text search, and yearly analytics. Explain how derived stores stay synchronized without becoming independent sources of truth.
exercise.answer: Use a transactional source for enrolment invariants, object storage for large media, a search index for text retrieval, and an analytical store when broad scans justify one. These are workload-based candidates rather than mandatory products. Define authoritative ownership, change propagation, rebuildability, freshness, access control, and failure recovery for derived indexes and reports.

units.label: 06A
units.title: Model architecture and estimate execution cost
units.shortTitle: Model architecture and estimate execution cost
units.description: Use architectural views and execution graphs to estimate software cost before implementation.

chapters.title: Choose what the architecture model must explain
paragraphs: An architectural model records selected design decisions, not every fact about the program. Components, connectors, interfaces, configurations and rationale answer different stakeholder questions. The web-system examples show how a cache, application, database, object store and external services can be placed in a shared picture. The important question is what each element and edge means and which decision the picture helps evaluate.

Choose detail and formality according to the benefit of creating and maintaining the model. Include constraints on interaction, concurrency or behavior when those constraints matter. Static structure and runtime state are different perspectives, although a running system can also change topology through scaling or redeployment. Functional and quality concerns can both be modeled; “prints medical records” leaves speed and confidentiality unresolved until the description specifies relevant conditions and evidence.
chapters.prediction: Is a more detailed model always more useful?
chapters.explanation: No. Detail incurs maintenance and cognitive costs; select what answers consequential stakeholder questions.
chapters.narration: Architecture modeling makes selected decisions explicit. Start with the question, then choose components, relationships, constraints and rationale that answer it. More detail is not automatically better. The model must remain understandable and maintainable, while preserving the assumptions needed to evaluate behavior and quality. Treat runtime state and structural organization as related but distinct perspectives.
chapters.focus: Choose what the architecture model must explain

chapters.title: Estimate before committing to implementation
paragraphs: Performance modeling can reveal a costly design before a full system exists. Execution graphs estimate scenario work; queueing networks estimate contention; other approaches can use simulation or learned relationships. Models allow early comparison of alternatives and resource needs, but their answers remain conditional on assumptions about operations, infrastructure and workload. A plausible model is an engineering aid rather than a performance guarantee.

Execution models in this unit omit resource contention. Their service costs therefore provide a baseline, not the response a busy production system must achieve. Finding an unacceptable baseline is valuable because queueing will not rescue it. Passing that check does not prove adequate loaded performance. Combine early models with prototypes and subsequent measurements, revising parameters as evidence becomes available instead of treating modeling and testing as mutually exclusive stages.
chapters.prediction: If an execution graph predicts 100 ms without contention, is 100 ms guaranteed under concurrent users?
chapters.explanation: No. Queueing, interference and model omissions can increase response time.
chapters.narration: Use early models to challenge a design while change is still affordable. An execution graph estimates required work without contention, making it useful for spotting obvious problems. A good baseline does not establish loaded performance. Refine assumptions with prototypes and measurements, then add queueing or simulation when competition for resources matters.
chapters.focus: Estimate before committing to implementation

chapters.title: Reduce execution graphs
paragraphs: Execution graphs make a scenario’s control flow explicit. Basic nodes represent processing steps; expanded nodes refer to another graph. Repetition nodes specify loops, case nodes select alternatives, parallel-and-join nodes wait for all branches and division nodes start work that need not finish before continuation. These distinctions determine whether work contributes directly to the response being measured.

Reduce simple structures while preserving the chosen metric. Sequential times add, a fixed loop multiplies its body cost by the repetition count and a case uses the minimum, maximum or probability-weighted average according to the question. Parallel elapsed time can depend on the longest branch only under assumptions about available resources and synchronization. Keep best path separate from best resource conditions: an average path without contention is still not an average loaded response.
chapters.prediction: Two exclusive branches take 10 and 90 ms with probabilities .9 and .1. What is expected branch cost?
chapters.explanation: 0.9×10+0.1×90=18 ms, plus any case-node overhead.
chapters.narration: An execution graph describes sequencing, repetition, alternatives and concurrency. Reduce each structure using the metric you intend to estimate. A probability-weighted case answers an average-path question, while minimum and maximum answer different questions. Keep parallel work and asynchronous work distinct, and remember that a no-contention graph has not yet accounted for waiting behind other requests.
chapters.focus: Reduce execution graphs

chapters.title: Translate software actions into resource demand
paragraphs: A basic operation may request abstract software services such as server work, database access and messaging. An overhead matrix maps each service unit onto CPU instructions, disk operations and network messages. Multiplying requested service units by that matrix yields resource quantities, which are then converted into time using device-specific service costs. Carry units through every multiplication to avoid confusing instructions with thousands of instructions.

The authorization illustration combines 3,110 CPU units at .00001 seconds, fourteen disk operations at .02 seconds and one network operation at .01 seconds. The total no-contention service time is .3211 seconds, approximately .32 seconds. These costs can also become device demands for a later queueing model. Keep the per-device vector as well as the scalar sum, because equal total work can create very different bottlenecks on different resources.
chapters.prediction: Why retain separate CPU, disk and network demand after summing execution time?
chapters.explanation: A contention model needs each resource’s demand to identify utilization and bottlenecks; the scalar total loses that information.
chapters.narration: The overhead matrix connects software actions to hardware work. First count resource quantities, then multiply by service time with consistent units. Summing provides a simple baseline, while the resource vector supports later contention analysis. Two designs with the same baseline time can behave differently under load if they concentrate work on different devices.
chapters.focus: Translate software actions into resource demand

chapters.title: Work through the ATM transaction scenario
paragraphs: The final exercise combines validation, one transaction branch and result delivery. Using the displayed matrix, validation costs .07315 seconds, withdrawal .0723, deposit .0986, balance inquiry .03715 and result delivery .01115. The shortest path is .12145 seconds and longest .1829 seconds under the given no-contention assumptions. The weighted average additionally depends on which probability belongs to each branch.

The printed solution assigns .001 to deposit, .7 to withdrawal and .299 to balance inquiry, yielding .14611645 seconds. The extracted diagram text does not unambiguously establish the edge mapping, so retain that mapping as an explicit assumption until visually checked. Compare the result with alternative probabilities to show workload sensitivity. End the exercise by identifying which resource costs and arrival assumptions are still needed before claiming performance under concurrent use.
chapters.prediction: Can we compute the expected path from branch times without knowing which probability belongs to each branch?
chapters.explanation: No. A sum of probabilities equal to one is insufficient; each probability must be paired with the correct branch.
chapters.narration: The ATM workshop turns graph reduction into a complete baseline estimate. Combine validation, a selected transaction and result delivery. State the branch-probability mapping rather than silently inferring it from extracted labels. The resulting average is conditional on that mapping and omits contention, so use it as input to further analysis rather than a production latency guarantee.

quiz.answer: Division starts work that need not all complete before continuation; a join waits for every attached branch.

quiz.answer: Evidence about contention, workload, model fidelity and measurement under relevant conditions.

review.correction: A system can dynamically reconfigure topology; design models may capture behavior. Performance tests and prototypes can occur early. Teach complementary perspectives rather than fixed lifecycle rules.

units.label: 06B
units.title: Queueing networks and architectural performance
units.description: Measure demand, utilization and response time with explicit queueing-model assumptions.

chapters.title: From execution cost to resource contention
paragraphs: A software execution model estimates the resources a scenario demands without competition from other requests. A queueing model adds that competition. A service station contains waiting work and one or more servers, where a server might represent a processor, disk or network link rather than a physical computer. Residence time includes both waiting and service; service time measures the resource work alone.

Kendall notation records assumptions about arrivals, service times, server count, capacity, population and scheduling. In the slide example, total capacity twenty includes three jobs in service and seventeen waiting. State this convention explicitly because “buffer” is ambiguous. Model choices matter: bursty arrivals, finite populations and priority scheduling can produce different behavior even when average service demand is unchanged. A useful model is precise about its boundary and assumptions.
chapters.prediction: Does a two-millisecond service demand imply a two-millisecond response at high load?
chapters.explanation: No. Waiting behind other work adds residence time even if the service demand is unchanged.
chapters.narration: Begin with the distinction between doing work and waiting for a resource. Execution models estimate demand; queueing models account for contention. Define the station boundary, number of servers and capacity convention before using a formula. The same average service time can yield very different response times when arrivals, scheduling or competing workloads change.
chapters.focus: From execution cost to resource contention

chapters.title: Measure throughput and apply operational laws
paragraphs: An execution profile records arrivals, completions and busy intervals over a measurement period. For the supplied twenty-second observation, eight completions yield throughput 0.4 jobs per second and sixteen busy seconds yield utilization 0.8. Average service demand is two seconds per completed job under the accounting assumptions. These measurements describe different quantities; utilization is a fraction, throughput is a rate and residence time is a duration.

The utilization law connects throughput and service demand, U=X×S for a single service resource. Little’s law relates average jobs inside a boundary to throughput and average residence time, N=X×R. Use consistent boundaries and a stable observation regime; do not mix system throughput with a device queue length. The NFS exercise completes 10,800 requests in 1,800 seconds, giving six per second; three active requests imply average residence of half a second.
chapters.prediction: A single encoding device is busy 40% of the time at 800 frames/s. A firmware change reduces mean service per frame to 0.3 ms. What mean service time did the measurements imply before the change, and what utilization is predicted afterward?
chapters.explanation: Before: S=U/X=.40/800=.0005 seconds, or 0.5 ms per frame. After: U=800×.0003=.24, or 24%, assuming the throughput and device boundary stay the same. Lower utilization alone does not establish an end-to-end latency target.
chapters.narration: Compute each metric with its units attached. Eight completions over twenty seconds means 0.4 jobs per second, while sixteen busy seconds means eighty percent utilization. Operational laws connect these measurements when their boundaries agree. Little’s law uses average jobs, throughput and residence time; it is not restricted to exponential arrivals or service.
chapters.focus: Measure throughput and apply operational laws

chapters.title: Understand single and multiple server queues
paragraphs: The M/M/1 model assumes Poisson arrivals, independent exponentially distributed service times and one server with an unbounded waiting room. In steady state it requires arrival rate λ below service rate μ. Its utilization is ρ=λ/μ, mean residence time is 1/(μ−λ), and mean jobs is ρ/(1−ρ). These expressions describe long-run averages under the model, not deterministic limits on individual requests.

Birth–death balance explains the geometric state distribution. At an empty system, departure rate is zero; at nonempty states it is μ. Multiple servers change departure capacity to min(n,m)μ and require a different waiting calculation such as Erlang C. Finite buffers change the model again: an infinite-queue tail probability is not automatically the exact blocking probability of a bounded system. Always define whether capacity includes the job being served.
chapters.prediction: What happens to M/M/1 residence time as λ approaches μ from below?
chapters.explanation: It grows without bound in the model; the stable formula cannot be used at or above capacity.
chapters.narration: M/M/1 provides a simple explanation for sharply increasing delay near saturation. Its assumptions and stability condition are part of the result. Birth–death balance gives state probabilities, while additional servers or finite buffers require changed calculations. Distinguish average delay, queue-tail probability and actual blocking rather than treating them as interchangeable measures of performance.
chapters.focus: Understand single and multiple server queues

chapters.title: Build an open queueing network
paragraphs: An open network receives external requests, routes them among resources and eventually releases them. A request may visit a device repeatedly. If external arrival rate is λ and average visits are V, device throughput is λV. Multiplying by service time per visit gives utilization. Total demand D=VS separates how often a resource is used from the cost of each use.

Under the simplified single-server station assumptions, each device contributes D/(1−λD) to request response time. Sum these contributions using consistent per-request accounting, and calculate average system population as λR. The ATM example exposes nonlinear scaling: doubling arrival rate increases CPU utilization from 0.468 to 0.936 when CPU visits are twenty-six. Corrected response rises from about 0.447 seconds to 2.699 seconds, rather than simply doubling. The source arithmetic needs repair before reuse.
chapters.prediction: At two transactions/s, 4.5 disk visits per transaction and 20 ms per visit, what are disk throughput and utilization?
chapters.explanation: Disk throughput is 9 I/O/s; utilization is 9×0.02=0.18, or 18%.
chapters.narration: Trace requests through resources and count visits. Device throughput differs from external request throughput when a request visits repeatedly. Convert visits and service time into demand, then calculate utilization and response under the chosen model. The ATM example shows why doubling arrivals near a bottleneck can increase delay much more than twofold.
chapters.focus: Build an open queueing network

chapters.title: Closed populations and model construction
paragraphs: A closed model keeps a fixed population circulating through the modeled workload. Interactive users alternate between thinking and requesting service; their next request depends on completing the previous cycle. An open model instead specifies arrivals from outside. Mixed models can contain both classes. Choosing the workload model is a behavioral decision, not a cosmetic change in how the same diagram is drawn.

To derive a queueing model from execution results, identify resource stations, connect their routes, choose the workload population or arrival rate and estimate service demand. Preserve whether quantities are per visit or per request. Check sensitivity to uncertain inputs and report average-model limitations. In the authorization example, CPU demand 0.0311 seconds and utilization 0.0933 give a CPU response contribution near 0.0343 seconds, exposing the source’s factor-of-ten error before computing the system total.
chapters.prediction: Does a fixed group of users who wait for each response generate a constant external arrival rate independently of delay?
chapters.explanation: No. Their request rate changes with response and think times; a closed interactive model captures that coupling.
chapters.narration: Choose open, closed or mixed workload behavior before solving the network. Fixed users with think time differ from independent external arrivals. Map execution demands onto stations and keep per-visit and per-request quantities distinct. Then vary uncertain parameters, identify the limiting resource and communicate what an average-value model does not predict about bursts or tail latency.
chapters.focus: Closed populations and model construction

chapters.title: End-to-end ATM modeling workshop
paragraphs: The processTransaction exercise combines execution-graph analysis with resource contention. First compute each operation’s resource demand from its software requests and the overhead matrix. A server action, database access and message can each consume several hardware resources, so a database operation is not merely one unit of disk time. Reduce sequential steps and probability-weighted alternatives to a per-request resource-demand vector.

Next apply the supplied ten-jobs-per-second workload and check every device utilization before calculating delays. If any modeled station reaches or exceeds capacity, report that the steady-state formula is inapplicable rather than displaying a negative response. The extracted text includes an unfinished worked solution and does not fully establish which branch probability labels attach to which nodes. Verify the diagram or explicitly state the assumed mapping before producing numerical answers.
chapters.prediction: If the reduced disk demand is 0.12 seconds/request at ten requests/s, can the single-server stable formula be applied?
chapters.explanation: No. Utilization would be 1.2; the assumed single disk station cannot sustain the offered workload.
chapters.narration: This workshop connects the two performance-modeling units. Convert operation requests through the overhead matrix, reduce the execution graph and obtain demand at each device. Apply arrival intensity only after that step. Check stability first, and do not hide ambiguous branch labels: state the mapping you use or obtain it from the original diagram.
chapters.focus: End-to-end ATM modeling workshop

quiz.question: A team applies the steady-state M/M/1 response formula at 60 jobs/s with mean service 20 ms. What must you flag before accepting its answer?
quiz.answer: Utilization is 60×.020=1.2. The infinite-buffer M/M/1 station has no finite steady-state mean at this load; a negative value from S/(1−λS) is not a valid response time. Reduce admitted load or increase effective service capacity.

quiz.question: Why cannot device throughputs simply be added to obtain external throughput?
quiz.answer: Each request may visit multiple devices or repeat visits; adding device completions double-counts request work.

quiz.question: A stable processing stage completes 120 jobs/s with mean in-system time 80 ms. Its dashboard labels 9.6 as the mean number waiting. What is wrong with that label?
quiz.answer: Little’s law gives 120×.080=9.6 jobs inside the whole measured stage, including jobs receiving service. It is not the waiting-only population. Use waiting-only time for a waiting-queue population or subtract the measured mean number in service.

units.label: 07A
units.title: REST APIs & serialization
units.description: Design resource operations with clear retry semantics, and turn data structures into valid network representations.

chapters.title: HTTP as an API contract
paragraphs: An API specifies how another program requests work and interprets results. HTTP-based APIs use methods, targets, fields, status codes and optional bodies. The weather example combines a location parameter with a JSON response. A useful contract documents units, missing values and errors as well as the successful payload.

Choose methods according to their semantics: GET retrieves a representation, PUT creates or replaces state at a known target, POST asks a resource to process supplied content, and DELETE removes the target association. Status codes help clients distinguish success, missing resources, forbidden access and server failure. HTTPS protects transport; avoid putting credential examples in URLs that may be logged or copied.
chapters.prediction: Is a JSON body alone enough to specify a reliable API contract?
chapters.explanation: No. Methods, resource identity, status/error behavior, authentication and data meaning also matter.
chapters.narration: An API is a contract, not merely a JSON document. Read the weather request as a combination of method, target, headers and body, and interpret the response using status and representation. Document units and errors as carefully as success. HTTP conventions let clients and infrastructure cooperate when the API follows their semantics.
chapters.focus: Methods, status codes, weather request, inputs and outputs.

chapters.title: Retries and resource identity
paragraphs: Retries are normal when a client cannot tell whether an operation completed. Idempotence means repeating an identical request has the same intended server effect as sending it once. It does not require the same response status. Deleting an already removed resource may report that it is missing without deleting anything else.

The delete-latest example fails this requirement because the target changes after the first deletion. A stable post identifier lets retries refer to the same item. Similarly, a PUT to a chosen document ID replaces that target, while POST creation may allocate a fresh ID each time unless the application provides deduplication. Resource-oriented naming helps communicate intent, but nouns alone do not define the REST architectural style.
chapters.prediction: After a timeout, is retrying DELETE /posts/latest as safe as DELETE /posts/42?
chapters.explanation: No. Latest may now identify a different post, whereas 42 remains the same target.
chapters.narration: Use a lost-response scenario to understand idempotence. The operation may already have happened when the client retries. Stable resource identity makes repeated PUT or DELETE requests predictable. Compare deleting the latest post with deleting a specific post, and remember that different response codes can still accompany the same idempotent server effect.
chapters.focus: Idempotence, delete-latest trap, stable IDs and resource-oriented design.

chapters.title: Serialization and references
paragraphs: Serialization turns structured values into bytes that can cross a network or be stored. JSON provides objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. XML uses elements and attributes with well-formed syntax. Correct examples matter: JSON forbids trailing commas, and an empty XML element must close explicitly or use self-closing syntax.

An in-memory graph is not always a simple nested tree. Repeating shared objects wastes space, and recursively nesting a cycle never ends. Emit each object once with an identifier, then encode relationships using those identifiers. Readers resolve references under an agreed schema. The byte dump illustrates ASCII-compatible UTF-8 text; characters beyond ASCII may require multiple bytes, so character count and byte count can differ.
chapters.prediction: What happens if Jess includes Tom, Tom includes Kate, and Kate includes a fully nested Jess?
chapters.explanation: Naive recursive serialization never terminates; IDs turn the cycle into finite references.
chapters.narration: Serialization bridges program structures and transmitted bytes. JSON and XML work well for trees, but shared references and cycles require an explicit representation. Encode each person once and link friends by ID. Validate syntax and distinguish characters from bytes: the ASCII example uses one byte per character, while UTF-8 supports wider characters too.
chapters.focus: Valid JSON/XML, bytes, duplication, cycles and ID references.

chapters.title: Choosing a protocol
paragraphs: HTTP offers widely available clients, servers, status semantics and caching infrastructure. HTTPS adds encrypted transport. Reuse can lower implementation effort, but API authors must understand caching and retry semantics instead of treating HTTP as an arbitrary message tube. Framework capabilities differ, so database pooling or deployment security should not be assumed automatically.

Separate architectural style, serialization and transport. REST describes architectural constraints; JSON and Protocol Buffers encode data; gRPC is an RPC framework that commonly uses Protocol Buffers with HTTP/2. Binary encoding therefore does not imply avoiding HTTP. Choose based on interoperability, tooling, streaming, payload size and measured performance requirements. Smaller messages alone do not settle the architecture decision.
chapters.prediction: Does choosing Protocol Buffers imply that the service cannot use HTTP?
chapters.explanation: No. gRPC commonly uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2.
chapters.narration: Choose technologies at the correct layer. HTTP is a protocol, JSON and Protocol Buffers serialize data, and gRPC provides an RPC framework. REST describes architectural constraints. Reusing HTTP infrastructure is useful, but its semantics remain part of the contract. Decide using compatibility and operational requirements, supported by measurement where performance matters.
chapters.focus: Reuse of HTTP infrastructure and distinction between serialization and transport.

quiz.answer: After the first deletion, latest points to a different post. Retry may delete again. Use a stable identifier such as DELETE /posts/42.
quiz.question: Why can DELETE /posts/latest violate DELETE idempotence, and what endpoint fixes it?

quiz.answer: No. The intended effect remains that the same resource is absent; response status need not stay identical.
quiz.question: A DELETE retry returns 404 after the first call returned 204. Does that prove non-idempotence?

quiz.answer: Emit each person once with a stable person_id and represent friendships with best_friend_id references; resolve IDs when reading.
quiz.question: How do you serialize Jess -> Tom -> Kate -> Jess without infinite nesting?

review.issue: Every HTTP method except POST is idempotent; identical result is required.
review.correction: Idempotence concerns the intended server effect of repeated identical requests, not identical responses. Safe methods plus PUT and DELETE are idempotent; do not assume PATCH is. A retry of DELETE can return a different status.

review.issue: Custom headers are frowned upon; verbs in paths define whether RESTful; PUT is always better.
review.correction: Teach noun-oriented resource naming as useful guidance, not the formal definition of REST. Standard headers are preferred when applicable; extension fields are legitimate. POST creation and PUT replacement fit different resource-ID ownership models.

review.issue: API keys in query URLs are shown as ordinary authentication.
review.correction: Use HTTPS and an appropriate authorization header in teaching examples; query credentials can leak through logs and copied URLs.

review.issue: XML hometown tag is unclosed; HTML is asserted to be XML.
review.correction: Use <hometown city="Seattle"/> or an explicit matching end tag. HTML and XML have distinct syntax rules.

review.issue: HTML is an XML document.
review.correction: Ordinary HTML uses HTML syntax; an XML serialization is separately supported.

review.issue: Each UTF-8 character is one byte.
review.correction: The ASCII characters shown use one byte each; UTF-8 encodes Unicode code points using one to four bytes.

review.issue: JSON example includes a trailing comma after hometown_id.
review.correction: Remove the trailing comma; valid JSON does not allow it.

review.issue: Protocol Buffers is a network API transport that does not use HTTP.
review.correction: Protocol Buffers is a serialization format/schema system. gRPC commonly combines it with HTTP/2, so binary encoding does not imply avoiding HTTP.

review.issue: Live third-party demo endpoints may be stale.
review.correction: Use self-contained fictional examples instead of requiring Twitter or obsolete homework endpoints; do not claim these old links were verified.

exercise.prompt: Design creation and deletion operations for submissions so a client can safely retry after a timeout. Include resource identifiers, statuses, authentication, and valid JSON.
exercise.answer: Use stable identifiers or an idempotency key with a defined deduplication lifetime. PUT to a client-chosen stable resource can support retry-safe creation if the semantics fit; POST can also support application-level idempotency. DELETE a stable submission ID, not a moving “latest” target. Define authorization and conflicts. Validate JSON without trailing commas and distinguish protocol semantics from payload format.

units.label: 07B
units.title: Microservices & client architectures
units.description: Compare a modular monolith with independently deployed services, accounting for contracts, failures, and team coordination.

chapters.title: One deployable application
paragraphs: A monolith is one application deployment boundary, even when many identical instances run behind a load balancer. The MediaWiki example makes this clear: two hundred interchangeable replicas improve capacity without dividing business responsibilities into distinct services. External databases and caches do not by themselves change that application boundary.

A monolith can simplify local execution, integration and transactions. Its challenges can include coordinating many contributors and deploying a large application for a small change. These are tradeoffs rather than inevitable defects: strong module boundaries can support a maintainable monolith. Evaluate the team, change patterns and operational needs before introducing network boundaries simply to make a diagram look more distributed.
chapters.prediction: Does adding a second identical application instance create a second microservice?
chapters.explanation: No. It creates another replica of the same application.
chapters.narration: Distinguish replication from decomposition. Replicas run the same application to serve more requests; microservices divide responsibilities into separately deployable components. A monolith often simplifies development and transactions. Its suitability depends on the system and team, so begin with concrete change and coordination problems rather than assuming more services are automatically better.
chapters.focus: Replicated monoliths, dependencies, development and deployment tradeoffs.

chapters.title: Choosing service boundaries
paragraphs: Service boundaries assign responsibilities to separate deployable applications. Each exposes a contract that clients can use without knowing its implementation language. This can enable specialized scaling and independent development, but only when changes can actually occur independently. A set of services that must always release together retains strong coupling.

Network boundaries introduce latency and partial failures. A successful payment with a failed inventory update cannot automatically be undone by a local database rollback. Designs need explicit retry, idempotence and recovery behavior. Debugging also crosses process boundaries. Smaller units may simplify focused tests while increasing the importance of contracts, observability and integration testing. Use business responsibilities and consistency requirements to justify a split.
chapters.prediction: If every service release requires all other services to release simultaneously, what promised benefit is weakened?
chapters.explanation: Independent deployment; the system retains release coupling despite network separation.
chapters.narration: Choose service boundaries around responsibilities and change patterns. Network APIs hide implementation details, but calls can fail independently and cross-service data updates require deliberate recovery. Compare the gain in independent deployment with the added testing and operational burden. A service split is justified when those benefits matter enough to pay the coordination cost.
chapters.focus: Specialized services, network contracts, failure and transaction costs.

chapters.title: Teams, mocks and multiple clients
paragraphs: Teams can agree on an API before implementing each side. A mock dependency lets client work proceed, but a mock represents assumptions rather than proof of compatibility. Define inputs, outputs, status behavior and error cases, then test those expectations against the real service. Instant, always-successful mocks hide timeouts and failures that matter in production.

The same backend API can support a browser, mobile app and desktop app. In a server-rendered design the backend prepares HTML; in an SPA much presentation logic runs in the browser and obtains data through APIs. Real applications can combine both approaches. Separating clients from services helps reuse, while authorization and validation must still be enforced by the server for every client type.
chapters.prediction: If a browser validates an input, can a shared backend trust the mobile client to do the same?
chapters.explanation: No. Each client can behave differently or be bypassed; the backend enforces its own contract and authorization.
chapters.narration: An explicit service contract allows teams to build clients and servers in parallel. Mocks help early work, and real integration tests check the assumptions they encode. A shared API can support web, mobile and desktop experiences. Compare server rendering and SPAs as presentation choices, while keeping backend validation and access control consistent.
chapters.focus: Parallel development, contract fidelity, SPAs and shared backend APIs.

quiz.answer: No. Replicas of the same deployable application provide scale; microservices divide responsibilities across independently deployable services.
quiz.question: A deployment has 200 interchangeable app replicas behind a load balancer. Is it necessarily a microservice architecture?

quiz.answer: One service may succeed while another fails or times out. A cross-service workflow needs explicit consistency and recovery choices, such as idempotent retries and compensating actions.
quiz.question: Checkout calls separate inventory and payment services. Why is failure handling harder than a single-database transaction?

quiz.answer: Contract edge cases, error/status behavior, timeouts, latency, version compatibility and integration with the real implementation.
quiz.question: A mock service returns correct JSON but always succeeds immediately. What important tests are missing?

review.issue: Monolith requires one language and necessarily becomes messy.
review.correction: A monolith is a deployment/architecture choice; modular monoliths can have strong boundaries and mixed-language components. Code quality and coordination costs depend on implementation and organization.

review.issue: Microservices are only a rebranding of SOA.
review.correction: Describe them as a related service-oriented approach emphasizing independently deployable services and bounded responsibilities, not an exact synonym.

review.issue: REST, Thrift, ProtoBuf, GraphQL are interchangeable API formats.
review.correction: These occupy different layers: REST is an architectural style; Protocol Buffers is a serialization/schema system; gRPC is an RPC framework that commonly uses it.

review.issue: Smaller services make testing easy and independent work guaranteed.
review.correction: Unit tests may simplify; contract, integration, failure, and end-to-end tests remain essential. Shared schemas or synchronized releases can recreate tight coupling.

review.issue: Named product architectures read as current facts.
review.correction: Use generic server-rendered and SPA examples; preserve the explicit caveat that many applications combine both.

exercise.prompt: A small team plans a new course-registration application. Compare a modular monolith with separate registration, payment, and notification services. Choose a starting design and define evidence that would justify changing it.
exercise.answer: A modular monolith can keep local transactions and deployment simple while enforcing internal boundaries. Independent services may be justified by distinct ownership, scaling, or release needs, but require network contracts, observability, and partial-failure handling. Payment and registration coordination must be explicit. State team constraints and measure actual bottlenecks before treating distribution as an automatic improvement.

units.title: Load balancing
units.description: Trace requests through local balancers, safe deployments, DNS, CDNs, and anycast.

review.issue: Health checks, buffering, protocol support, and throughput need qualification.
review.correction: Failed probes are evidence, reverse proxies can stream, and rates depend on workload and implementation.

review.issue: Cache directives and time conversions need correction.
review.correction: private excludes shared caches; no-cache requires validation; max-age=0 is immediately stale; 31,622,400 seconds is 366 days.

review.correction: Routing policy and topology determine paths; global services retain capacity and failure constraints.

units.label: 08B
units.title: Push notifications and connected clients
units.description: Connect devices, choose a delivery channel, and route notifications across changing connections.

chapters.title: Why the server cannot simply call the phone
paragraphs: A ride arrival or an auction bid happens because another participant acts. The recipient needs an update without repeatedly asking whether anything changed. Yet a phone is not an ordinary public server: its address changes, NAT and firewalls restrict inbound connections, and the application may be suspended. Email and SMS provide useful notification channels, but do not replace every in-app interaction.

The architectural requirement is therefore a reachable delivery path, not merely an HTTP endpoint on the device. An outbound connection can establish that path while the device is online. Offline periods still require a policy for retaining, expiring or replacing messages. Distinguish notifying a person from synchronizing the authoritative state: a missed alert should not erase the underlying ride or bid.
chapters.prediction: Would assigning a phone a REST endpoint guarantee that a backend can reach it?
chapters.explanation: No. Address changes, NAT, firewalls and offline periods remain obstacles.
chapters.narration: A ride arrival or an auction bid happens because another participant acts. The recipient needs an update without repeatedly asking whether anything changed. Yet a phone is not an ordinary public server: its address changes, NAT and firewalls restrict inbound connections, and the application may be suspended. Email and SMS provide useful notification channels, but do not replace every in-app interaction.
chapters.focus: NAT, reachability and event origin

chapters.title: Registration and mobile delivery
paragraphs: Mobile push services let an application backend address a registered app instance through platform infrastructure. The app obtains a provider-issued identifier and sends it to its authenticated backend. Later, the backend associates an event with the relevant installations and submits a notification. The operating system manages the delivery connection, avoiding a separate continuously active connection for every installed application.

Treat registration identifiers as changeable routing information rather than permanent user identities. A user can own multiple devices, and a device installation can receive a new identifier. Update registration records and remove invalid destinations. Provider acceptance is not proof of display or user attention; retention limits, connectivity and device policy affect delivery. Use notifications to prompt a state refresh when correctness matters.
chapters.prediction: A push provider accepts a request. Has the user necessarily seen it?
chapters.explanation: No. Acceptance, device receipt, application processing and human attention are separate milestones.
chapters.narration: Mobile push services let an application backend address a registered app instance through platform infrastructure. The app obtains a provider-issued identifier and sends it to its authenticated backend. Later, the backend associates an event with the relevant installations and submits a notification. The operating system manages the delivery connection, avoiding a separate continuously active connection for every installed application.
chapters.focus: Registration lifecycle and best-effort delivery

chapters.title: WebSockets, long polling and alternatives
paragraphs: An active browser can open a WebSocket and exchange messages in both directions while the connection remains alive. Long polling instead leaves an HTTP request pending until data or a timeout arrives, then starts another request. Both permit an update to arrive without a fresh user action. Their latency and operational behavior differ from repeatedly making short periodic polling requests.

Choose transport from communication needs. Server-sent events provide a server-to-browser stream over HTTP; WebSockets support bidirectional messages. Browser background Web Push is a separate mechanism from an open page connection. Every active connection can break, so design reconnection, authentication renewal and recovery of missed state. A timeout such as sixty seconds is an implementation choice, not part of the definition of long polling.
chapters.prediction: Does a WebSocket by itself replay messages missed during a disconnected interval?
chapters.explanation: No. Replay or state resynchronization belongs to the application protocol.
chapters.narration: An active browser can open a WebSocket and exchange messages in both directions while the connection remains alive. Long polling instead leaves an HTTP request pending until data or a timeout arrives, then starts another request. Both permit an update to arrive without a fresh user action. Their latency and operational behavior differ from repeatedly making short periodic polling requests.
chapters.focus: Transport choice and reconnect behavior

chapters.title: Routing to the correct connection
paragraphs: A distributed notification service must find the worker holding each live client connection. Other backend services should send a logical user notification rather than guess the physical socket owner. A registry connects user and installation identities to provider destinations or live connection identifiers. This allows the notification service to serve multiple devices and browser tabs without duplicating routing logic across domain services.

Connection records become stale when clients disconnect or workers fail. Remove obsolete entries, renew registrations and tolerate races between lookup and delivery. A managed gateway may expose a connection identifier rather than a raw socket address; the same lifecycle problem remains. Store durable business state separately so reconnecting clients can recover even when transient delivery fails, and authorize both subscription and outbound routing.
chapters.prediction: Steve has two browser tabs and one phone. Should the registry contain only one destination?
chapters.explanation: No. It needs the intended set of current destinations, with per-connection or per-installation lifecycle handling.
chapters.narration: A distributed notification service must find the worker holding each live client connection. Other backend services should send a logical user notification rather than guess the physical socket owner. A registry connects user and installation identities to provider destinations or live connection identifiers. This allows the notification service to serve multiple devices and browser tabs without duplicating routing logic across domain services.
chapters.focus: Notification service registry and fan-out

quiz.question: Why is a push token not a permanent user ID?
quiz.answer: It identifies a provider destination or app installation and can change; the backend maps current destinations to an authenticated user.

quiz.question: When is SSE a useful alternative to WebSockets?
quiz.answer: When the active client chiefly needs a server-to-client event stream; bidirectional application messaging may favor WebSockets.

quiz.question: What should a client do after reconnecting following a missed seat-availability alert?
quiz.answer: Retrieve authoritative current availability or replay from a supported cursor; do not infer state from the missing alert alone.

review.issue: Permanent device identity and simple IP registration model.
review.correction: Present provider tokens/identifiers as changeable app-instance routing data, not permanent user identities; platform internals are simplified.

review.issue: GCM names and browser transport choices are historical.
review.correction: Use Firebase Cloud Messaging terminology and include SSE and background Web Push as distinct options; WebSockets are not universally preferred.

review.issue: Connection ownership without recovery details.
review.correction: A connection registry needs expiry/cleanup and reconnect handling; push delivery is not proof of durable application state.

exercise.prompt: Design delivery for course cancellation alerts to a phone and two browser tabs. Include offline behavior.
exercise.answer: Maintain authorized per-user installation and connection records; send through mobile providers or owning WebSocket workers; use message IDs and expiry; clean stale registrations; clients fetch authoritative course status on reconnect.

units.label: 08C
units.title: Queueing networks — alternate slide version
units.description: Revisit the queueing model using the alternate deck, with consistent CPU visit counts and corrected arithmetic.

chapters.title: From execution cost to resource contention
paragraphs: A software execution model estimates the resources a scenario demands without competition from other requests. A queueing model adds that competition. A service station contains waiting work and one or more servers, where a server might represent a processor, disk or network link rather than a physical computer. Residence time includes both waiting and service; service time measures the resource work alone.

Kendall notation records assumptions about arrivals, service times, server count, capacity, population and scheduling. In the slide example, total capacity twenty includes three jobs in service and seventeen waiting. State this convention explicitly because “buffer” is ambiguous. Model choices matter: bursty arrivals, finite populations and priority scheduling can produce different behavior even when average service demand is unchanged. A useful model is precise about its boundary and assumptions.
chapters.prediction: Does a two-millisecond service demand imply a two-millisecond response at high load?
chapters.explanation: No. Waiting behind other work adds residence time even if the service demand is unchanged.
chapters.narration: Begin with the distinction between doing work and waiting for a resource. Execution models estimate demand; queueing models account for contention. Define the station boundary, number of servers and capacity convention before using a formula. The same average service time can yield very different response times when arrivals, scheduling or competing workloads change.
chapters.focus: From execution cost to resource contention

chapters.title: Measure throughput and apply operational laws
paragraphs: An execution profile records arrivals, completions and busy intervals over a measurement period. For the supplied twenty-second observation, eight completions yield throughput 0.4 jobs per second and sixteen busy seconds yield utilization 0.8. Average service demand is two seconds per completed job under the accounting assumptions. These measurements describe different quantities; utilization is a fraction, throughput is a rate and residence time is a duration.

The utilization law connects throughput and service demand, U=X×S for a single service resource. Little’s law relates average jobs inside a boundary to throughput and average residence time, N=X×R. Use consistent boundaries and a stable observation regime; do not mix system throughput with a device queue length. The NFS exercise completes 10,800 requests in 1,800 seconds, giving six per second; three active requests imply average residence of half a second.
chapters.prediction: A storage device is busy 60% of the time while completing 150 operations/s. A proposed index makes each request use three such operations instead of two. At the same request rate, what utilization do you predict if per-operation service cost is unchanged?
chapters.explanation: The current request rate is 150/2=75 requests/s, and mean device service per operation is .60/150=.004 s. Three visits give 225 operations/s and utilization 225×.004=.90. The extra index may speed reads elsewhere while pushing this device close to saturation.
chapters.narration: Compute each metric with its units attached. Eight completions over twenty seconds means 0.4 jobs per second, while sixteen busy seconds means eighty percent utilization. Operational laws connect these measurements when their boundaries agree. Little’s law uses average jobs, throughput and residence time; it is not restricted to exponential arrivals or service.
chapters.focus: Measure throughput and apply operational laws

chapters.title: Understand single and multiple server queues
paragraphs: The M/M/1 model assumes Poisson arrivals, independent exponentially distributed service times and one server with an unbounded waiting room. In steady state it requires arrival rate λ below service rate μ. Its utilization is ρ=λ/μ, mean residence time is 1/(μ−λ), and mean jobs is ρ/(1−ρ). These expressions describe long-run averages under the model, not deterministic limits on individual requests.

Birth–death balance explains the geometric state distribution. At an empty system, departure rate is zero; at nonempty states it is μ. Multiple servers change departure capacity to min(n,m)μ and require a different waiting calculation such as Erlang C. Finite buffers change the model again: an infinite-queue tail probability is not automatically the exact blocking probability of a bounded system. Always define whether capacity includes the job being served.
chapters.prediction: What happens to M/M/1 residence time as λ approaches μ from below?
chapters.explanation: It grows without bound in the model; the stable formula cannot be used at or above capacity.
chapters.narration: M/M/1 provides a simple explanation for sharply increasing delay near saturation. Its assumptions and stability condition are part of the result. Birth–death balance gives state probabilities, while additional servers or finite buffers require changed calculations. Distinguish average delay, queue-tail probability and actual blocking rather than treating them as interchangeable measures of performance.
chapters.focus: Understand single and multiple server queues

chapters.title: Build an open queueing network
paragraphs: An open network receives external requests, routes them among resources and eventually releases them. A request may visit a device repeatedly. If external arrival rate is λ and average visits are V, device throughput is λV. Multiplying by service time per visit gives utilization. Total demand D=VS separates how often a resource is used from the cost of each use.

Under the simplified single-server station assumptions, each device contributes D/(1−λD) to request response time. Sum these contributions using consistent per-request accounting, and calculate average system population as λR. The ATM example exposes nonlinear scaling: doubling arrival rate increases CPU utilization from 0.468 to 0.936 when CPU visits are twenty-six. Corrected response rises from about 0.447 seconds to 2.699 seconds, rather than simply doubling. The source arithmetic needs repair before reuse.
chapters.prediction: At two transactions/s, 4.5 disk visits per transaction and 20 ms per visit, what are disk throughput and utilization?
chapters.explanation: Disk throughput is 9 I/O/s; utilization is 9×0.02=0.18, or 18%.
chapters.narration: Trace requests through resources and count visits. Device throughput differs from external request throughput when a request visits repeatedly. Convert visits and service time into demand, then calculate utilization and response under the chosen model. The ATM example shows why doubling arrivals near a bottleneck can increase delay much more than twofold.
chapters.focus: Build an open queueing network

chapters.title: Closed populations and model construction
paragraphs: A closed model keeps a fixed population circulating through the modeled workload. Interactive users alternate between thinking and requesting service; their next request depends on completing the previous cycle. An open model instead specifies arrivals from outside. Mixed models can contain both classes. Choosing the workload model is a behavioral decision, not a cosmetic change in how the same diagram is drawn.

To derive a queueing model from execution results, identify resource stations, connect their routes, choose the workload population or arrival rate and estimate service demand. Preserve whether quantities are per visit or per request. Check sensitivity to uncertain inputs and report average-model limitations. In the authorization example, CPU demand 0.0311 seconds and utilization 0.0933 give a CPU response contribution near 0.0343 seconds, exposing the source’s factor-of-ten error before computing the system total.
chapters.prediction: Does a fixed group of users who wait for each response generate a constant external arrival rate independently of delay?
chapters.explanation: No. Their request rate changes with response and think times; a closed interactive model captures that coupling.
chapters.narration: Choose open, closed or mixed workload behavior before solving the network. Fixed users with think time differ from independent external arrivals. Map execution demands onto stations and keep per-visit and per-request quantities distinct. Then vary uncertain parameters, identify the limiting resource and communicate what an average-value model does not predict about bursts or tail latency.
chapters.focus: Closed populations and model construction

chapters.title: End-to-end ATM modeling workshop
paragraphs: The processTransaction exercise combines execution-graph analysis with resource contention. First compute each operation’s resource demand from its software requests and the overhead matrix. A server action, database access and message can each consume several hardware resources, so a database operation is not merely one unit of disk time. Reduce sequential steps and probability-weighted alternatives to a per-request resource-demand vector.

Next apply the supplied ten-jobs-per-second workload and check every device utilization before calculating delays. If any modeled station reaches or exceeds capacity, report that the steady-state formula is inapplicable rather than displaying a negative response. The extracted text includes an unfinished worked solution and does not fully establish which branch probability labels attach to which nodes. Verify the diagram or explicitly state the assumed mapping before producing numerical answers.
chapters.prediction: If the reduced disk demand is 0.12 seconds/request at ten requests/s, can the single-server stable formula be applied?
chapters.explanation: No. Utilization would be 1.2; the assumed single disk station cannot sustain the offered workload.
chapters.narration: This workshop connects the two performance-modeling units. Convert operation requests through the overhead matrix, reduce the execution graph and obtain demand at each device. Apply arrival intensity only after that step. Check stability first, and do not hide ambiguous branch labels: state the mapping you use or obtain it from the original diagram.

quiz.question: For a stable M/M/1 stage with 40 jobs/s and mean service 15 ms, a teammate claims mean residence is also 15 ms. Calculate the missing waiting contribution.
quiz.answer: Utilization is .6 and residence is .015/(1−.6)=.0375 s=37.5 ms. Mean waiting is 37.5−15=22.5 ms. Service time alone excludes queueing delay.

quiz.question: Why cannot device throughputs simply be added to obtain external throughput?
quiz.answer: Each request may visit multiple devices or repeat visits; adding device completions double-counts request work.

quiz.question: Twelve interactive users each wait two seconds for a response, then think for four seconds before submitting again. With one outstanding request per user and a stable cycle, what throughput is implied?
quiz.answer: X=N/(R+Z)=12/(2+4)=2 requests/s. Only XR=4 users on average are inside the request-processing system; the other eight are thinking. Do not use all twelve as the in-system population with response time alone.
