chapters.focus: Normalized model and explicit workload assumptions

chapters.title: Materialized feeds and asynchronous publication
paragraphs: A materialized feed moves work from reading time to publication time. When an author posts, workers add a reference or entry to followers’ prepared feeds. A reader can then fetch a bounded structure keyed by user. This suits a workload with many repeated reads, but each post now creates work proportional to the number of destinations receiving the update.

Asynchronous fan-out shortens the publisher’s wait by separating acceptance from completion; it does not eliminate the work. Use durable publication records, resumable fan-out batches and idempotent feed entries. A million-follower author can create a large backlog, so report realistic freshness and monitor lag. Store a canonical post and appropriate identifiers so deletion, moderation and updates can propagate without treating every copied entry as independent truth.
chapters.prediction: If one post targets ten million feeds, does returning immediately make those writes disappear?
chapters.explanation: No. It moves the work into a background pipeline and creates a freshness and recovery obligation.

A reader can then fetch a bounded structure keyed by user. This suits a workload with many repeated reads, but each post now creates work proportional to the number of destinations receiving the update.
chapters.focus: Fan-out cost and materialized views

chapters.title: Partitioning a social graph
paragraphs: Partitioning by follower can keep a person’s follow list and prepared feed together. It cannot simultaneously place every followed author’s original posts beside every reader without duplication. Social relationships cross partition boundaries, so a normalized read may fetch from several owners. The graph model makes the tension visible: balancing vertices and keeping related vertices together are competing objectives.

Distinguish data ownership from replica placement. Replication protects availability and may serve reads; denormalization creates a different access-oriented representation. Neither gives unlimited scaling without coordination, network cost or hotspots. Use a small graph of classmates and popular instructors to compare partition choices, count cross-partition reads and estimate update fan-out. That evidence is more useful than assigning all relational stores one performance profile.
chapters.prediction: Can placing an author’s post on one shard make it local to all followers on different shards?
chapters.explanation: No. Readers need remote access, replication or a derived copy; the placement conflict remains.

chapters.title: Hybrid feeds and the celebrity exception
paragraphs: A hybrid design precomputes updates for ordinary authors and merges selected high-fan-out authors’ recent posts when a reader opens the feed. This avoids sending every popular post to millions of inactive followers. The threshold is a workload decision: compare expected fan-out cost against the reads that would need an on-demand merge, including freshness and cache behavior for popular content.

The slides use a relational store for the popular-author path, but that is an illustrative choice rather than a requirement. Popular authors do not necessarily write more than their followers read; their distinguishing feature is amplification per post. A complete hybrid needs consistent ordering, pagination, duplicate suppression and deletion handling across both paths. Explain those merge rules before claiming the hybrid provides the best of every option.
chapters.prediction: What makes a celebrity post expensive in fan-out-on-write?
chapters.explanation: Its very large follower set, not necessarily a high posting rate or writes exceeding reads.

This avoids sending every popular post to millions of inactive followers. The threshold is a workload decision: compare expected fan-out cost against the reads that would need an on-demand merge, including freshness and cache behavior for popular content.
chapters.focus: Hybrid fan-out threshold and merge semantics

quiz.question: What work shifts when feeds are materialized?
quiz.answer: Repeated read-time joins/assembly are partly replaced by publication-time fan-out and ongoing view maintenance.

quiz.question: Why can asynchronous fan-out still violate a five-second freshness target?
quiz.answer: The queued workload may exceed processing capacity, especially for high-fan-out authors; acceptance is not completed propagation.

quiz.question: What must a hybrid feed do when the same post appears in both inputs?
quiz.answer: Merge with stable ordering and deduplicate by a canonical post identifier, while enforcing visibility and deletion rules.

review.issue: NoSQL equated to DHTs with perfect scaling and no coordination.
review.correction: This is an idealized partitioned key-value model, not a universal NoSQL guarantee; practical systems have skew, replication and membership overhead.

review.issue: SQL cannot handle large feeds; celebrity writes exceed reads.
review.correction: Performance comes from workload and materialization strategy. Celebrities cause high fan-out; SQL/NoSQL labels do not determine the trade-off.

review.issue: Exercise could be mistaken for real current Twitter architecture.
review.correction: Label all three versions hypothetical teaching designs; the slides themselves call the model theoretical.

exercise.prompt: For a campus feed with 30,000 students and an account followed by all of them, propose a hybrid and define failure recovery.
exercise.answer: Precompute ordinary-author entries; merge campus-wide announcements on read or cache their recent list. Use canonical IDs, stable ordering and bounded pagination; resume fan-out from durable progress and make insertions idempotent; propagate visibility changes and measure freshness.

units.label: 13A
units.title: Implicit invocation, pub/sub and event-driven systems
units.shortTitle: Implicit invocation, pub/sub and event-driven systems
units.description: Design event subscriptions, brokered delivery and recovery, then examine the ROS example.

chapters.title: From direct calls to implicit invocation
paragraphs: With a direct call, the caller names the operation it wants another component to perform. With implicit invocation, a component announces an event and registered handlers react. A debugger can announce that execution stopped, letting an editor highlight source without the debugger depending on that editor’s implementation. The same idea supports user-interface observers and database triggers inside a single application.

The connector determines dispatch semantics. An in-process event can invoke handlers synchronously, while a distributed event bus often delivers asynchronously. A publisher should not assume which subscribers exist or that they finish in a particular order unless the contract explicitly provides it. This enables extension and replacement, but makes the full chain of effects harder to see during debugging and error handling.
chapters.prediction: Must every implicit event invocation cross a network or run asynchronously?
chapters.explanation: No. A local connector can invoke handlers synchronously; distributed messaging is one specialization.
chapters.narration: With a direct call, the caller names the operation it wants another component to perform. With implicit invocation, a component announces an event and registered handlers react. A debugger can announce that execution stopped, letting an editor highlight source without the debugger depending on that editor’s implementation. The same idea supports user-interface observers and database triggers inside a single application.
chapters.focus: Event announcement versus direct dependency

chapters.title: Event-driven architecture and brokered fan-out
paragraphs: An event describes something that happened, such as a seat becoming available. Consumers can react independently: notify a student, update a dashboard or record an audit trail. A publisher-subscriber intermediary routes events to interested subscriptions, reducing the producer’s need to track every consumer address. Topics and filters let consumers select relevant changes without requiring a new direct integration for each interested service.

Decoupling does not erase contracts. Event fields, identifiers, versions and authorization rules remain shared responsibilities. Separate subscriptions can maintain their own progress, while competing workers within one subscription may share its load. Request/reply communication needs correlation identifiers and an explicit reply path when a caller requires a specific result. Choose that pattern deliberately rather than hiding a mandatory synchronous dependency behind an event.
chapters.prediction: If analytics and notifications both need each enrolment event, should they compete for a single work item?
chapters.explanation: No. They need independent subscriptions or equivalent fan-out so each receives the event stream.
chapters.narration: An event describes something that happened, such as a seat becoming available. Consumers can react independently: notify a student, update a dashboard or record an audit trail. A publisher-subscriber intermediary routes events to interested subscriptions, reducing the producer’s need to track every consumer address. chapters.title: Delivery, ordering and poison messages
paragraphs: Subscribers must plan for duplicates, failures and delayed delivery. An idempotent handler prevents repeated execution from creating an extra effect, but it does not make out-of-order changes safe. Include entity versions or process related events in an ordered partition when sequence matters. A priority queue changes which message runs first; it is not a substitute for preserving business-event order.

Repeatedly failing messages need bounded retries and a dead-letter workflow with diagnosis and controlled replay. Expiry prevents obsolete work from consuming resources, while scheduled availability postpones otherwise valid work. Monitor each subscription’s lag so one slow consumer is visible without blocking all others. Eventual consistency is an application choice with limits, especially when a stale view can authorize an irreversible action.
chapters.prediction: Does making a handler idempotent guarantee that version 4 cannot overwrite version 5?
chapters.explanation: No. Duplicate safety and ordering are different; compare versions or enforce the required sequence.
chapters.narration: Subscribers must plan for duplicates, failures and delayed delivery. An idempotent handler prevents repeated execution from creating an extra effect, but it does not make out-of-order changes safe. chapters.title: ROS as an architectural example
paragraphs: The robotics example organizes computation into nodes with typed messages. Topics carry streams such as sensor readings, services provide request-and-response interactions, and actions support longer goals with progress and a final result. These interfaces let sensing, planning, control and visualization evolve separately while still communicating through explicit data contracts suited to their interaction patterns and timing needs.

The central ROS Master in the slides describes ROS 1 naming and registration. ROS 2 commonly uses middleware discovery rather than that same central master architecture. Do not transfer every topology assumption across versions. A robot also requires deliberate delivery and timing policies: a fresh camera frame and an emergency stop do not have identical needs. Pub/sub modularity helps composition but does not establish safety by itself.
chapters.prediction: Would a long-running navigation goal with progress feedback fit best as a single sensor topic?
chapters.explanation: An action interface better expresses goal, feedback, cancellation/status and result; topics still carry ongoing observations.
chapters.narration: The robotics example organizes computation into nodes with typed messages. Topics carry streams such as sensor readings, services provide request-and-response interactions, and actions support longer goals with progress and a final result. chapters.focus: Topics, services, actions and ROS version scope

quiz.question: How does pub/sub differ from workers competing for jobs on one queue?
quiz.answer: Independent subscriptions each receive relevant events; competing workers share processing within a delivery group or queue.

quiz.question: Why does a dead-letter queue not complete error recovery by itself?
quiz.answer: Someone or some process must diagnose, correct and safely replay or discard the isolated message.

quiz.question: Which ROS interface suits a continuous sensor feed and which suits a long-running goal?
quiz.answer: A topic suits continuous observations; an action suits a goal with feedback and result.

review.issue: Broker automatically ensures delivery and priority queue fixes ordering.
review.correction: Delivery depends on retention, durability and acknowledgement settings; priority is distinct from event order, and idempotency handles duplicates rather than reorderings.

review.issue: Pub/sub implies eventual consistency.
review.correction: Pub/sub can support eventually consistent views, but the required application guarantees and repair mechanisms must be specified.

review.issue: ROS Master presented as all ROS.
review.correction: Explicitly label ROS 1; distinguish ROS 2 middleware discovery.

exercise.prompt: Design enrolment events consumed by email, analytics and a seat-count projection. Include one poison-message scenario.
exercise.answer: Publish a versioned event with unique ID and course/student identifiers after durable enrolment. Use separate subscriptions; email deduplicates, analytics tracks progress, and the projection enforces entity order/version. Retry transient failures with limits; isolate an invalid schema message, alert, repair and replay safely.

units.label: 13B
units.title: Batch, streaming and two leader–follower patterns
units.shortTitle: Batch, streaming and two leader–follower patterns
units.description: Compare batch and streaming computation, thread handoff and replicated-log leadership.

chapters.title: Distributed aggregates and data movement
paragraphs: Serving independent requests is different from calculating one answer over a large shared dataset. For a global maximum, each worker can compute a local maximum and send one candidate to a coordinator. The coordinator takes the maximum of those candidates, so little data moves. Other operations need richer summaries or repeated communication, making network cost part of algorithm design rather than an incidental implementation detail.

For a mean, combine sums and counts instead of averaging unequal-sized partitions’ means. Exact median selection is more involved: a pivot-based algorithm counts values below, equal to and above the pivot and narrows the target rank. Duplicates and even-sized inputs require explicit treatment. Hardware bandwidth examples provide lower bounds only under stated assumptions; use decimal petabytes consistently or label binary units correctly.
chapters.prediction: Can we average each month’s average order value to obtain the overall average?
chapters.explanation: Only when counts are equal. In general combine total sums and counts.
chapters.narration: Serving independent requests is different from calculating one answer over a large shared dataset. For a global maximum, each worker can compute a local maximum and send one candidate to a coordinator. The coordinator takes the maximum of those candidates, so little data moves. chapters.focus: Associative summaries, ranks and bandwidth bounds

chapters.title: MapReduce and finite batch jobs
paragraphs: MapReduce asks a programmer to transform input records into intermediate key-value pairs, then combine values sharing a key. For word counting, the mapper emits one pair per word occurrence and the reducer sums counts for each word. The shuffle groups intermediate data by key. Scheduling, distribution and retries belong largely to the framework, so the program can focus on the transformations.

A batch job works on a bounded input and eventually finishes; it does not imply sequential execution. Multiple tasks can run in parallel, and several jobs can be chained through intermediate results. Data locality can reduce traffic, but shuffle still transfers information among workers. A skewed key can overload a reducer, and retried tasks mean side effects outside the framework need careful design.
chapters.prediction: What happens if the mapper returns immediately on the first word inside its loop?
chapters.explanation: It counts only the first word; it must emit or accumulate a pair for every occurrence.

For word counting, the mapper emits one pair per word occurrence and the reducer sums counts for each word. The shuffle groups intermediate data by key. chapters.title: Continuous streams and state
paragraphs: Stream processing reacts to an ongoing sequence rather than waiting for a complete dataset. Monitoring and recommendations may benefit from short update latency, while historical reporting can tolerate larger batch intervals. Low latency is a target, not an automatic guarantee. A stream operator may still wait for enough evidence, and overloaded consumers can accumulate lag even when the architecture is called real time.

Stateful stream computations need rules for windows, late arrivals, duplicates and recovery. Distinguish event time from the time a processor receives the event. The slides introduce Storm through sources and processing components; treat ease-of-operation and feature comparisons as contextual rather than universal. Compare batch and streaming on freshness, boundedness and operational requirements, not on the assumption that one handles large data and the other does not.
chapters.prediction: If yesterday’s event arrives today, which daily count should include it?
chapters.explanation: The answer depends on the stated event-time and lateness policy; processing-time grouping would put it in today’s arrival window.

chapters.title: The thread-pool Leader/Followers pattern
paragraphs: The Leader/Followers concurrency pattern coordinates a pool of threads waiting for events. One thread leads by waiting on an event source; when an event arrives, another follower can become leader while the previous leader handles the work. The purpose is efficient event dispatch with controlled coordination overhead, not replication of durable data across a cluster of machines.

Correct handoff protects shared event sources and avoids having every thread compete for the same notification. Benefits depend on workload and runtime, and a blocked handler still needs appropriate timeout or cancellation behavior. Do not import distributed consensus claims into this thread-pool pattern: a new leading thread is not equivalent to safely electing a database leader after a network partition. Distinguish the two before discussing fault tolerance.
chapters.prediction: Does promoting another waiting thread provide replicated durability after machine failure?
chapters.explanation: No. Thread leadership manages local concurrency; durable distributed recovery is a separate design.

chapters.title: Kafka partition leaders and replicated logs
paragraphs: Kafka illustrates a different use of leader and follower terminology. A partition has a leader responsible for its log operations and replica followers that copy its data. Leadership can move after failure under a cluster coordination policy. Several partitions can distribute leadership across brokers, so one leader per partition does not mean the entire system has only one active writer.

Durability and availability depend on acknowledgements, in-sync replicas and election policy; replication alone is not an unconditional guarantee. A lagging replica may be unsuitable for safe promotion. The slides’ ZooKeeper control-plane account is historical, while Kafka 4 uses KRaft. For the e-commerce analytics example, distinguish ingestion durability from successful downstream computation and from committing external business effects exactly once.
chapters.prediction: May any follower be promoted without risking loss of acknowledged records?
chapters.explanation: No. Its synchronization state and the configured election and acknowledgement policies matter.

Leadership can move after failure under a cluster coordination policy. quiz.question: How do you compute a global mean from partitions with unequal record counts?
quiz.answer: Sum all partition sums and divide by the sum of their counts.

quiz.question: Why does batch processing not imply sequential processing?
quiz.answer: Batch refers to bounded input and a finishing job; many map/reduce tasks can execute in parallel.

quiz.question: How do the two leader–follower meanings differ?
quiz.answer: One coordinates event-handling threads locally; the other replicates partition logs across brokers and requires distributed failure policies.

review.issue: Old volume forecasts and incorrect units/arithmetic formatting.
review.correction: Mark forecasts historical. PB is 10^15 bytes; PiB is 2^50. With the assumed 80 GB/s, 10^16/(80×10^9)=125000 seconds, about 34.7 hours; do not assert a universal PCIe maximum.

review.issue: Mean and median oversimplified.
review.correction: Combine sums/counts for mean. Median selection needs target rank, equality handling and a defined even-cardinality policy.

review.issue: return inside word loop stops mapping early.
review.correction: Emit each (word,1) pair or return a completed list after the loop.

review.issue: Batch sequential and product feature judgments universal.
review.correction: Bounded batch work can be parallel; treat Storm feature/operability claims as version- and workload-dependent.

review.issue: Thread pattern conflated with distributed replica leadership.
review.correction: Teach them separately; local thread promotion is not distributed consensus or machine-failure durability.

review.issue: ZooKeeper is the current Kafka coordinator.
review.correction: Label historical; Kafka 4.0 uses KRaft and removed ZooKeeper mode.

review.issue: Replication guarantees consistency and availability without qualification.
review.correction: State acknowledgements, in-sync replica and election assumptions; end-to-end processing needs its own correctness contract.

exercise.prompt: Design enrolment analytics with a nightly historical report and a live dashboard. Explain recovery and the leadership pattern involved.
exercise.answer: Run a bounded batch aggregation for the historical report and a stateful streaming projection for the dashboard. Partition events by an appropriate entity, define event-time/late-data handling, checkpoint progress and make outputs replay-safe. Broker partition leaders replicate logs; a local event-loop thread pool, if used, solves a different concurrency problem.
